questions.question: You ask a patient, "What's wrong today?" and she answers, "I've had chest pressure since breakfast." For your report, her answer - the reason she called for help, in her own words - is recorded as her:

Nod, keep eye contact, and say, "Go on - tell me more about that."
Ask, "When you say it popped, do you mean a sound or a feeling?"
Say, "So you believe the wrist is broken, then."
questions.explanation: Encouraging the patient to provide more information - "go on, tell me more," with attentive body language - is facilitation. Repeating his words back is reflection, asking what he meant by them is clarification, and telling him what he believes is interpretation; none of those opens the door the way facilitation does.

choices: Diabetes mainly affects wound care after transport; it has no effect on pain perception, circulation, or blood glucose during a call of this length.
Diabetes heightens pain perception, so her reported pain likely overstates her injuries; her glucose is also unlikely to change after only a few hours without food, so it does not need checking.

Diabetic peripheral neuropathy blunts pain perception, so her injuries (possible hip or pelvis fracture, with crepitus noted) may be worse than her reported pain suggests; assess beyond the pain score. After roughly 7 hours without food or medication, check her blood glucose for hypoglycemia. Poor circulation also slows healing.
Her diabetes is unrelated to this fall, since it is controlled by diet alone and does not affect sensation in the extremities.

questions.question: Dispatch describes a "minor fall," so you walk in picturing a quick lift assist. Instead you find the patient pale, sweating, and clutching his chest - and for a moment you keep treating it as a fall call. The picture in your head that you walked in with is your:

choices: Introduce yourself, get to her eye level, make gentle eye contact, listen without interrupting, explain each step before you do it, and speak in a calm, unhurried tone
Stand back and avoid eye contact so she feels less watched, and let your partner do all the talking while you work
Direct your explanations to her adult daughter, since the patient is too upset to take anything in
Use proper medical terms for everything so she can see the crew is knowledgeable, and reassure her she will make a full recovery
questions.explanation: Therapeutic communication means introducing yourself, making eye contact, listening actively without interrupting, showing empathy, explaining every procedure before you do it, and using a calm tone - techniques that encourage the patient to open up. Avoiding the patient, hiding behind medical jargon, or talking only to family members all shut communication down.
questions.question: You are caring for an 86-year-old woman who fell into her bathtub. She is embarrassed and withdrawn, answering you in whispers and avoiding your eyes. Which approach is most likely to help her open up and work with the crew?

choices: Online medical control - the radio consultation you held with the hospital before treating
A verbal order - the physician's spoken instruction given during this call

questions.explanation: Standing orders are written documents, signed by the medical director, that give directions and permissions in advance, so no call is needed. A verbal order and online medical control both require contacting the physician during this call, which you did not do.
questions.question: Your patient qualifies for a medication under your system's written care guidelines, so you give it right away without calling the hospital for permission first. You are able to do this because of:

The patient's full name and date of birth, so registration can start
The street address you are responding from, so the hospital can log where the call came from
Your estimated time of arrival, so the hospital knows when to have the room and team ready
questions.explanation: The initial report's key job is to let the hospital prepare, and the one item it must carry is your estimated time of arrival. The patient's name, the address you came from, and your opinion of the diagnosis do not belong in that first radio report.
questions.question: Your crew is 10 minutes from the hospital with a patient whose condition is getting worse. You key the radio to give your initial report so the hospital can get ready. Which piece of information must that first report get across above all?

choices: Slow down, get to his eye level, and try to see the situation from his side - he is watching his brother hurt and feels helpless
Ignore him completely and push the call forward so the situation resolves itself
Assert your authority firmly and tell him the crew takes orders from no one on scene
Call for law enforcement first and stop all communication until they arrive
questions.explanation: When communicating in a crisis, it is vital to consider the perspective of the other person - fear and helplessness are driving his behavior. Establishing your authority or exerting your influence escalates the conflict; seeing his side is what calms the scene and keeps communication open.

Mainly so the dispatcher can bill the call correctly and assign the run number; field care is not affected by dispatcher communication.

choices: No. Never lie to a patient or invent an answer. Misinformation breaks the patient's trust, can distort her decisions about her own care, and creates ethical and legal exposure. Reduce anxiety with honest reassurance and clear explanations instead.
Yes, but only when the patient is elderly or confused, because accurate information would upset them more than it helps.

choices: Whether anyone on scene is violent, whether there are hazards such as gas odors, and whether the patient may have something contagious - plus whether she is conscious and breathing adequately
Only the address and a callback number, so questions do not delay the response
Her insurance information and preferred hospital, so the admission paperwork can start
A complete medical history and a full set of vital signs, taken by the caller before you arrive
questions.explanation: The dispatch information that changes how you prepare is scene safety first: a possible infectious disease (so you bring PPE), environmental hazards such as odors or carbon monoxide (fire department), or violence risk (law enforcement) - then whether the patient is conscious and breathing, plus age and sex if possible. Billing details can wait, and a caller cannot supply a reliable history or vital signs.
questions.question: You are responding at night to an "unknown illness" call about an 83-year-old woman. Before you arrive, which set of questions should the dispatcher be asking the caller so your crew walks in prepared?

questions.explanation: A cellular telephone is a low-power radio that communicates through an interconnected series of repeater stations called cells, handing the call off as you move. A base station is fixed hardware at one location; a scanner only receives and cycles through channels; a repeater rebroadcasts one signal on a second frequency.
questions.question: Driving across town, your portable phone never loses its signal. Without you doing anything, it hands the call off from one low-power repeater site to the next as you move. This works because the phone is a:

questions.explanation: The MED channels are the VHF and UHF channels the Federal Communications Commission designated exclusively for EMS use. A trunked talk group is assigned from a shared pool of frequencies, simplex is a one-direction-at-a-time mode, and paging channels carry alerts - none of those are reserved for EMS.
questions.question: You need to call in a report to the hospital, and the regular traffic channels are jammed with fire and police calls. You switch to the set of VHF and UHF frequencies the federal regulators set aside for EMS use only. You are now transmitting on:

choices: First determine the degree of hearing loss; hearing aids may let her hear normally. Do not assume deafness or low intelligence. Position yourself so she can see your lips and facial expressions; never shout in her ear. Ask short questions and give short answers, and listen carefully. If aids fail, a stethoscope in her ears while you speak into the diaphragm can amplify sound. If speech fails, write questions down; a family member may interpret, and basic sign language ('hurt,' 'sick,' 'help') helps.
Rely mainly on her family to answer for her, because direct communication with a hearing-impaired patient is usually unsuccessful.
Avoid written notes and gestures, since they can confuse older patients; instead, keep explanations brief and move on if she does not respond.
Speak as loudly as possible directly into her ear, since volume is the main barrier, and repeat each question several times until she answers.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.
questions.question: YOU are the Provider (83-year-old woman, lightheadedness and nausea): How can you maximize successful communication with a patient who is hard of hearing?

choices: "Pt c/o n/v, hx HTN, DM, COPD, s/p CABG, NKDA, txp via ALS, ETA 10."
"Patient found seated on couch, pale and diaphoretic, complaining of nausea. Skin cool to touch. Denies chest pain. Vitals as charted."
"Patient seemed to be exaggerating her symptoms and was probably looking for attention more than help."
"Responded from the station on Elm Street after the tones dropped; crew of three on board."
questions.explanation: A narrative should record physical assessment findings - what you saw, heard, and measured - in plain, objective language. Your opinions about the patient do not belong in the report, a wall of abbreviations buries the findings, and response logistics say nothing about the patient's condition.
questions.question: You are finishing the narrative section of your report for this call. Which narrative entry documents the call the way a narrative should?

questions.explanation: repeater: A special base station radio that receives messages and signals on one frequency and then automatically retransmits them on a second frequency.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: A special base station radio that receives messages and signals on one frequency and then automatically retransmits them on a second frequency.

questions.explanation: Understanding and managing your own emotions, and responding well to the emotions of others, is emotional intelligence. Rapport is the trusting relationship you build with a patient; facilitation is encouraging a patient to keep talking; ethnocentrism is treating your own culture as more important than another's.
questions.question: After a rough call, your partner snaps at you over something small. You feel your own temper rising, recognize it, take a breath, and answer calmly instead of snapping back. What have you just used?

questions.explanation: An interoperable communications system uses voice-over-Internet Protocol (VoIP) technology so multiple agencies can share voice, data, and other communication in a disaster. Trunking only assigns frequencies within one system; paging sends alerts; telemetry transmits patient data.
questions.question: At a tornado disaster, fire, EMS, and law enforcement crews from three counties can all talk to each other and share data, even though each agency normally uses its own system. The shared system that links them uses Internet-based voice technology and is called:

choices: Limit the interview to yes-or-no questions, avoid eye contact so the patient does not feel pressured, and finish as quickly as possible.
Stand over the patient while asking questions, avoid touch, and discuss the patient's condition with your partner in front of her to save time.

Look directly at the patient and speak slowly and distinctly. Do not raise your volume unless the patient has hearing loss. Use nonverbal communication clues and touch as appropriate. Never talk about the patient in front of her; it implies she has no say in her care and can escalate her fear of losing independence.
Speak quickly and raise your volume so the patient can follow along, and direct most questions to family members who can answer more clearly.
questions.explanation: From the book's printed YOU are the Provider summary.
questions.question: YOU are the Provider (83-year-old woman, lightheadedness and nausea): What techniques can facilitate the process of interviewing an older patient?

choices: Mostly administrative questions: her insurance carrier, her preferred pharmacy, the name of her employer, and who will pay for the transport.

How long she was in the tub and how she was extricated; her mental and neuro status; signs of hypothermia and what warming was done; her blood glucose; medications, allergies, and last food or medication; pulse, motor, and sensory function after immobilization; and any other injuries found.
Questions about your agency's protocols, staffing, and response times rather than the patient's condition.
Only questions about the radio report itself, such as your unit number and the time you left the scene.
questions.explanation: Answer written from the chapter (no printed key).
questions.question: Navigate Case Study (86-year-old woman, fall into bathtub): What questions do you anticipate emergency department personnel to ask?

questions.explanation: multiplex: The ability to transmit audio and data signals through the use of more than one communications channel.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: The ability to transmit audio and data signals through the use of more than one communications channel.

questions.explanation: chief complaint: The reason a patient called for help; also, the patient’s response to questions such as “What’s wrong?” or “What happened?”
questions.question: Which term is defined as: The reason a patient called for help; also, the patient’s response to questions such as “What’s wrong?” or “What happened?”

choices: Speak as quickly and loudly as possible so the report is finished before you reach the hospital
State early in the report that this is an "alert" patient, so the hospital can assemble the team before you arrive
Use code words for the patient's condition to protect her identity over the air
Give every detail you have, in the order you discovered it, before mentioning the alert
questions.explanation: When a patient meets alert criteria, mention that this is an "alert" level patient as soon as possible in the report so the receiving team can be ready. Detail still matters, but burying the alert wastes exactly the preparation time the alert system exists to save.
questions.question: You are transporting a patient who meets your system's criteria for an "alert" activation at the hospital. When you radio your report to the hospital, you should:

questions.explanation: Sending a radio signal carrying a voice or digital alert to a belt receiver is paging. A mobile data terminal message appears on the terminal mounted in the ambulance; telemetry transmits patient data such as an ECG; trunking is computer assignment of frequencies.
questions.question: At 2 a.m., tones sound at the station and a dispatcher's voice message is sent out to the small receiver clipped to your belt, alerting your crew to a call. This alerting method is called:

questions.explanation: Cultural imposition is imposing your own beliefs, values, and practices on another person because you believe your ideals are superior. Ethnocentrism is the attitude of judging your culture superior; imposition is the act of forcing your practices on the patient.
questions.question: A patient declines a treatment step for religious reasons. Your partner insists anyway, telling the family, "We do it our way - it's better," and pushes his own practices on them over their objections. Your partner is guilty of:

choices: A billing document in both cases, since payment disputes drive all record requests
A legal record of the care given, and then a source for quality improvement and training
A dispatch log of response times, and then a vehicle maintenance record
A personal journal for the crew, and then a scheduling tool for future shifts
questions.explanation: The PCR serves several functions: it is the written record of the event and the care given, medical documentation the hospital can reference, information for other providers, a record of care and supplies used, a tool for quality improvement and training, and a record for medical and legal issues. The subpoena uses the legal function; the quality review uses the quality improvement function.
questions.question: Six months after a call, your patient care report is subpoenaed for a court case. A month later, your agency's quality team pulls the same report to review how the crew handled the call. In each case, the report is doing its job as:

questions.explanation: A receiver that searches across several frequencies and locks onto an active transmission is a scanner. A repeater rebroadcasts signals on a second frequency; a base station is the fixed transmitter and receiver at headquarters; multiplex sends voice and data on separate channels at once.
questions.question: The radio at your station base keeps cycling through several channels on its own. Whenever a transmission starts on one of them, it stops there until the message ends, then starts cycling again. This receiver is a:

questions.explanation: On simplex, a single frequency carries transmissions in one direction at a time; while you transmit, you cannot receive, so two people transmitting at once lose both messages. Duplex lets transmitting and receiving happen at the same time; multiplex sends voice and data on separate channels; trunking assigns frequencies from a pool.
questions.question: You and your partner are talking on portable radios at a scene. Every time you both key up at the same moment, neither of you hears a word the other said. This happens because your radios are operating in:

questions.explanation: emotional intelligence: The ability to understand and manage one’s own emotions and properly respond to the emotions of others.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: The ability to understand and manage one’s own emotions and properly respond to the emotions of others.

questions.explanation: A health information exchange is the shared system that lets providers access a patient's health data - past problems, medications, allergies - and avoid duplicating tests. The mobile data terminal is only the screen in the ambulance that displays the information; the patient care report is the legal record your crew creates for this call.
questions.question: Before you arrive, the screen in your ambulance pulls up a frequent patient's medication list, allergies, and past medical problems from records shared between hospitals and EMS agencies, so you do not repeat tests she had yesterday. The system that supplied this information is a:

questions.explanation: A base station is radio hardware containing a transmitter and receiver located in a fixed place - headquarters. A repeater's job is narrower: it receives a signal on one frequency and rebroadcasts it on a second frequency; a scanner only receives; a cellular telephone is a low-power portable.
questions.question: Every transmission from your crews funnels through the powerful transmitter and receiver mounted at headquarters, which never moves and coordinates the whole system's traffic. That fixed installation is the:

choices: Keep explanations to a minimum and rely on gestures alone, since spoken details are causing the confusion
Speak more loudly and repeat each instruction several times until she gets it right
Use standard medical abbreviations and jargon so your wording matches the terminology the hospital uses
Use plain words, keep sentences short, face her while you speak, and ask her to repeat key points back to you
questions.explanation: To minimize miscommunication, use plain words instead of jargon, keep sentences short and clear, speak slowly, face the patient, and confirm understanding by having key points repeated back. Louder repetition, jargon, and gestures alone all leave the misunderstanding in place.
questions.question: An 86-year-old patient keeps misunderstanding your instructions during care - she nods, then does the opposite of what you asked. Which approach is most likely to fix the communication problem?

choices: Sit at her eye level, make eye contact, and say, "You seem worried. Tell me what's on your mind."
Stand over her and explain that staying quiet will only slow down her care.
Ask yes-or-no questions as fast as you can so the interview stays on track.
Avoid eye contact and work silently so she does not feel pressured.
questions.explanation: Therapeutic communication uses verbal and nonverbal techniques that encourage a patient to express her feelings. Eye contact, sitting at her level, and an open invitation to talk do that; standing over her, avoiding her, or firing closed questions at her all shut communication down.
questions.question: A 40-year-old patient with abdominal pain has gone quiet and is staring at the floor, answering you in one-word replies. Which response is most likely to get her talking again?

questions.explanation: documentation: The recorded portion of the EMT’s patient interaction, either written or electronic. This becomes part of the patient's permanent medical record.
questions.question: Which term is defined as: The recorded portion of the EMT’s patient interaction, either written or electronic. This becomes part of the patient's permanent medical record.

choices: "How often does a situation like this occur?" - checking how common the call type is
"Which hospital is closest?" - deciding where the call ends up
"What category does this patient fit into?" - settling on a label for the patient
"What got us to this point in care?" - retracing how the call reached this state
questions.explanation: To establish a mental model, it is vital to answer "What got us to this point in care?" - rebuilding the story of the call so the new findings fit into it. A category label, how often the situation occurs, and the closest hospital do not rebuild your picture of what is happening with this patient.
questions.question: Halfway through a call, the patient's condition changes and nothing matches the picture your crew formed at the start. To rebuild an accurate picture of the situation, which question should the crew work through first?
